name: Gross margin
description: Computes the gross margin as revenue minus cost of goods sold, divided by revenue: (revenue − cogs)/revenue. It shows the fraction of sales left after direct production costs.
notes: The result is a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. It covers only cost of goods sold, not operating, tax, or other expenses.

name: Net profit margin
description: Computes the net profit margin as net income divided by revenue. It shows the fraction of each sales dollar that remains as profit after all expenses and taxes.
notes: The result is a decimal, so multiply by 100 for a percentage. Unlike gross margin, this accounts for all costs including operating expenses, interest, and taxes.

name: Return on equity (ROE)
description: Divides net income by shareholder equity to measure return on equity, showing how much profit a company generates from each unit of owners' capital.
notes: Result is a fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Use net income for the period and equity from the same basis; high leverage can inflate ROE without more efficiency.

name: Return on assets (ROA)
description: Divides net income by total assets to give return on assets, indicating how efficiently a company uses its assets to generate profit.
notes: Result is a fraction; multiply by 100 for a percentage. Use net income for the period; ROA varies widely across industries, so compare only within a sector.

name: Debt-to-equity ratio
description: Divides total debt by total equity to give the debt-to-equity ratio, a leverage measure showing how much borrowing a company uses relative to owners' capital.
notes: A ratio of 1 means debt equals equity. Definitions of debt vary (total liabilities vs. interest-bearing debt only), so state which is used when comparing companies.

name: Current ratio
description: Divides current assets by current liabilities to give the current ratio, a liquidity measure of a company's ability to cover short-term obligations with short-term assets.
notes: A ratio above 1 means current assets exceed current liabilities. Very high values may signal idle cash or excess inventory rather than strong liquidity.

name: Quick ratio
description: Subtracts inventory from current assets and divides by current liabilities to give the quick (acid-test) ratio, a stricter liquidity measure using only assets easily turned into cash.
notes: Inventory is excluded because it is hardest to liquidate quickly. A ratio of 1 means liquid assets just cover current liabilities; compare against the current ratio to gauge inventory reliance.

name: Retention Ratio
description: Calculates the share of net income kept in the business rather than paid out, as one minus the dividend payout ratio, expressed as a percentage. It is the plowback rate that funds internal growth.
notes: This is the complement of the payout ratio, so the two sum to 100 percent. Net income must be positive for a meaningful result; a higher retention rate supports reinvestment over distributions.

name: Sustainable Growth Rate
description: Multiplies return on equity by the retention ratio (one minus the payout ratio) to estimate how fast a firm can grow using only retained earnings, without new equity. The result is a percentage per year.
notes: Enter ROE and payout as decimals. It assumes constant margins, asset use, and leverage, and no new share issuance; growing faster generally requires external financing.

name: Interest Coverage Ratio
description: Divides earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) by interest expense to show how many times operating profit covers interest payments. A value of 8 means EBIT is eight times the interest owed.
notes: A higher ratio signals a greater cushion for servicing debt; values near or below 1 warn that operating profit barely covers interest. Interest must be positive for the ratio to be meaningful.

name: Gross Profit Margin
description: Subtracts cost of goods sold from revenue, divides by revenue, and multiplies by 100 to show the percentage of sales remaining after direct production costs. It measures core production profitability.
notes: This covers only direct costs of goods sold, not operating, interest, or tax expenses. Revenue must be positive; compare within an industry since typical margins vary by sector.

name: Operating Margin
description: Divides operating income by revenue and multiplies by 100 to show the percentage of each sales dollar left after operating expenses. It gauges profitability from core operations, before interest and taxes.
notes: Operating income excludes interest and tax but includes overhead beyond direct costs, so it sits below gross margin. Revenue must be positive for a meaningful percentage.

name: Cash Ratio
description: Adds cash and marketable securities and divides by current liabilities, measuring the firm's ability to cover short-term obligations using only its most liquid assets. A value of 0.72 means liquid assets cover 72 percent of current liabilities.
notes: This is the strictest liquidity ratio, excluding receivables and inventory. A very high value may signal idle cash; current liabilities must be positive for a meaningful result.

name: Working Capital
description: Subtracts current liabilities from current assets to show the short-term liquid capital available to fund day-to-day operations. A positive figure means current assets exceed obligations due within a year.
notes: This is an absolute amount, not a ratio, so scale it against firm size when comparing. Negative working capital can indicate liquidity stress or, in some business models, efficient supplier financing.

name: Debt Ratio
description: Divides total debt by total assets to show the proportion of a company's assets financed by debt. A value of 0.44 means 44 percent of assets are funded through borrowing rather than equity.
notes: A higher ratio means greater financial leverage and risk. Definitions of debt vary (total liabilities versus interest-bearing debt only), so confirm which is used before comparing firms.

name: Equity Multiplier
description: Divides total assets by total equity to measure how much of the firm's assets are supported by each unit of shareholder equity. A value of 1.8 means assets are 1.8 times equity, with the rest funded by liabilities.
notes: It is a leverage measure: higher values mean more debt financing and greater risk. Equity must be positive; negative equity makes the multiplier meaningless.

name: Return on Capital Employed (ROCE)
description: Divides EBIT by capital employed (total assets minus current liabilities) and multiplies by 100, showing operating profit generated per unit of long-term capital. It measures how efficiently capital produces returns.
notes: Uses pre-interest, pre-tax profit so it is independent of financing structure. Capital employed must be positive; compare over time or against peers as absolute levels vary by industry.

name: Asset Turnover
description: Divides revenue by total assets to show how many units of sales the firm generates per unit of assets. A value of 0.56 means each dollar of assets produces 56 cents of revenue.
notes: Higher turnover signals more efficient use of assets to generate sales. It varies widely by industry, so compare only among similar businesses; ideally use average assets over the period.

name: Inventory Turnover
description: Divides cost of goods sold by average inventory to show how many times inventory is sold and replaced over the period. A value of 4 means stock cycles through roughly four times per year.
notes: Using COGS (not revenue) keeps numerator and denominator on a cost basis. Higher turnover suggests efficient inventory management, but too high may risk stockouts; average inventory must be positive.

name: Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO)
description: Multiplies average inventory by 365 and divides by cost of goods sold to estimate the average number of days inventory is held before being sold. Lower values mean stock moves faster.
notes: It is the inverse of inventory turnover expressed in days and assumes a 365-day year. Use average inventory and match COGS to the same period for accuracy.

name: Receivables Turnover
description: Divides revenue by average accounts receivable to show how many times the firm collects its receivables over the period. A value of 8.33 means receivables are collected roughly eight times per year.
notes: Higher turnover indicates faster collection of credit sales. Ideally use credit sales rather than total revenue, and average receivables; the denominator must be positive.

name: Days Sales Outstanding (DSO)
description: Multiplies average receivables by 365 and divides by revenue to estimate the average number of days it takes to collect payment after a sale. Lower values mean cash is collected sooner.
notes: It is the inverse of receivables turnover in days and assumes a 365-day year. For accuracy use credit sales and average receivables matched to the same period.

name: Payables Turnover
description: Divides cost of goods sold by average accounts payable to show how many times the firm pays off its suppliers over the period. A value of 6.67 means payables are settled roughly seven times per year.
notes: A higher ratio means faster payment to suppliers; a lower one means the firm holds cash longer. Use purchases or COGS consistently, and average payables; the denominator must be positive.

name: Days Payables Outstanding (DPO)
description: Multiplies average payables by 365 and divides by cost of goods sold to estimate the average number of days the firm takes to pay its suppliers. Higher values mean the firm holds onto cash longer.
notes: It is the inverse of payables turnover in days and assumes a 365-day year. Longer DPO improves cash flow but stretching too far may strain supplier relationships; match COGS to the period.

name: EBITDA Margin
description: Divides EBITDA by revenue and multiplies by 100 to show operating profitability before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, as a percentage of sales. A value of 26 percent means EBITDA is 26 percent of revenue.
notes: By excluding depreciation and amortization it approximates operating cash generation but ignores capital intensity and financing. Revenue must be positive; compare within an industry.

name: Times Interest Earned
description: Reconstructs EBIT by adding tax and interest expense back to net income, then divides by interest expense to show how many times pre-tax operating profit covers interest. A value of 5 means EBIT is five times the interest owed.
notes: Adding tax and interest back to net income rebuilds EBIT so the numerator is on a pre-interest, pre-tax basis. Interest expense must be positive; a value near 1 signals thin coverage.

name: Fixed Asset Turnover
description: Divides revenue by net fixed assets to measure how efficiently a company uses its plant, property and equipment to generate sales. A result of 1.56 means each currency unit of net fixed assets produces 1.56 units of revenue.
notes: Net fixed assets means value after accumulated depreciation. Higher is generally better, but norms vary by industry, so compare only within the same sector.

name: Operating Cash Flow Ratio
description: Divides operating cash flow by current liabilities to measure how well cash generated from operations covers short-term obligations. A ratio of 1.2 means operations produced 1.2 times the current liabilities in cash.
notes: A ratio above 1 indicates operating cash alone can meet current liabilities. It uses actual cash flow, so it is less exposed to accrual accounting distortions than the current ratio.

name: Internal Growth Rate
description: Computes the internal growth rate, the maximum rate a firm can grow using only retained earnings without external financing, ROA*b/(1 - ROA*b). It combines return on assets with the earnings retention ratio.
notes: ROA and b are decimals, with b the fraction of earnings retained (1 minus payout). The denominator must stay positive, so ROA*b must be less than 1.

name: Quick Ratio (Acid-Test)
description: Computes the quick (acid-test) ratio as current assets minus inventory, divided by current liabilities. It measures a firm's ability to meet short-term obligations using only its most liquid assets, excluding inventory that may be slow to convert to cash.
notes: Inventory is subtracted because it is the least liquid current asset; a stricter version also removes prepaid expenses. A ratio near or above 1 is generally considered healthy.

name: Operating Profit Margin
description: Computes the operating profit margin as operating income divided by revenue. It shows the proportion of each sales dollar remaining after covering operating expenses but before interest and taxes, reflecting core operating profitability.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). It excludes interest and taxes, so it isolates operating performance from financing and tax effects.

name: Net Profit Margin (Return on Sales)
description: Computes the net profit margin as net income divided by revenue. It measures the share of each sales dollar that becomes bottom-line profit after all expenses, including interest and taxes, have been deducted.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Unlike operating margin, it includes interest, taxes, and any non-operating items.

name: Inventory Turnover Ratio
description: Computes inventory turnover as cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. It indicates how many times a company sells and replaces its inventory over a period, reflecting how efficiently stock is managed.
notes: Use cost of goods sold (not sales) in the numerator and average inventory over the period; dividing 365 by this ratio gives average days inventory is held.

name: Receivables Turnover Ratio
description: Computes receivables turnover as net credit sales divided by average accounts receivable. It shows how many times a firm collects its average receivables during a period, indicating the effectiveness of credit and collection policies.
notes: Ideally the numerator is credit sales only, excluding cash sales; dividing 365 by this ratio gives the average collection period in days.

name: Total Asset Turnover
description: Computes total asset turnover as revenue divided by total assets. It measures how efficiently a company uses its entire asset base to generate sales, expressing sales produced per unit of assets.
notes: Often total assets is taken as an average of beginning and ending balances. A higher value means assets are used more efficiently, though typical levels vary widely by industry.

name: DuPont Identity (3-Step ROE)
description: Decomposes return on equity into the product of net profit margin, asset turnover, and the equity multiplier. This three-step DuPont identity shows how profitability, asset efficiency, and financial leverage together drive shareholder returns.
notes: Inputs are decimal ratios, and the result is ROE as a decimal (multiply by 100 for percent). The equity multiplier (assets/equity) captures leverage, so a high ROE may reflect debt rather than operating strength.

name: Extended DuPont (5-Step ROE)
description: Decomposes return on equity into five factors: tax burden, interest burden, operating margin, asset turnover, and the equity multiplier, multiplied together. This extended DuPont breakdown separates the effects of taxes and financing costs from operating performance and leverage.
notes: Tax burden is net income over pretax income, and interest burden is pretax income over EBIT; all inputs are decimals and the result is ROE as a decimal (multiply by 100 for percent).

name: Debt-to-Equity Multiple
description: Computes the debt-to-equity ratio as total debt divided by total equity. It measures financial leverage by showing how much debt financing the firm uses relative to shareholders' equity.
notes: Definitions of debt vary (total liabilities vs. interest-bearing debt only), so keep the numerator consistent. A value of 1 means debt equals equity.

name: Debt-to-Assets Ratio
description: Computes the debt-to-assets ratio as total debt divided by total assets. It indicates the proportion of a company's assets financed by debt, serving as a measure of leverage and solvency risk.
notes: The result is a fraction between 0 and 1 when debt does not exceed assets; a value above 1 signals negative equity. Keep the debt definition consistent with how assets are measured.

name: Equity-to-Assets Ratio
description: Computes the equity-to-assets ratio as total equity divided by total assets. It shows the share of assets funded by owners' equity rather than debt, indicating financial stability and the equity cushion available.
notes: This ratio is the complement of the debt-to-assets ratio when total assets equal debt plus equity, so the two sum to 1. A higher value means lower leverage.

name: Interest Coverage Ratio (Times Interest Earned)
description: Computes the interest coverage ratio (times interest earned) as EBIT divided by interest expense. It measures how many times a company's operating earnings can cover its interest obligations, gauging its ability to service debt.
notes: EBIT is earnings before interest and taxes; a higher ratio means a larger safety margin for interest payments. A value near or below 1 indicates earnings barely cover interest.

name: Debt Service Coverage Ratio
description: Computes the debt service coverage ratio as net operating income divided by total debt service. It measures whether operating income is sufficient to cover required principal and interest payments over a period.
notes: Debt service includes both principal and interest due; a ratio below 1 means income does not fully cover obligations. Lenders often require a minimum such as 1.2 or higher.

name: Net Working Capital
description: Computes net working capital as current assets minus current liabilities. It represents the short-term liquidity available to fund day-to-day operations after covering near-term obligations.
notes: A positive value indicates a liquidity buffer; a negative value can signal short-term funding pressure. This is an absolute currency amount, not a ratio.

name: Degree of Financial Leverage
description: Computes the degree of financial leverage as EBIT divided by EBIT minus interest expense. It measures how sensitively earnings per share (or net income) respond to a change in operating income, reflecting the effect of fixed financing costs.
notes: The denominator is pretax income; the larger the interest expense relative to EBIT, the higher the leverage. If interest equals or exceeds EBIT, the measure breaks down.

name: Degree of Combined Leverage
description: Computes the degree of combined leverage as the product of the degree of operating leverage and the degree of financial leverage. It measures the total sensitivity of earnings per share to a change in sales, combining operating and financial risk.
notes: It equals contribution margin divided by pretax income and captures both cost structure and financing effects. Inputs are the two component leverage factors as decimals.

name: Retention (Plowback) Ratio
description: Computes the retention (plowback) ratio as one minus dividends paid divided by net income. It is the fraction of earnings kept in the business rather than distributed to shareholders, funding reinvestment and growth.
notes: It is the complement of the dividend payout ratio, so the two sum to 1; the result is a decimal fraction. Multiplying it by return on equity gives the sustainable growth rate.

name: Altman Z-Score (Manufacturing)
description: Computes the Altman Z-score for manufacturing firms as a weighted sum of five financial ratios: working capital, retained earnings, and EBIT relative to assets, market equity to liabilities, and sales to assets. It is a composite predictor of bankruptcy risk.
notes: For this original model, a score above about 2.99 suggests safety and below about 1.81 signals distress; it applies to public manufacturers, with different coefficients for other firm types.

name: Defensive Interval Ratio
description: Computes the defensive interval ratio as the sum of cash, marketable securities, and receivables divided by daily operating expenses. It estimates how many days a firm can cover its operating costs using only its liquid defensive assets.
notes: The result is a number of days and excludes inventory; daily operating expense is typically annual cash operating costs divided by 365. It ignores any incoming revenue during the period.

name: Capital Intensity Ratio
description: Computes the capital intensity ratio as total assets divided by revenue. It measures how many units of assets are required to generate one unit of sales, indicating how asset-heavy a business is.
notes: It is the reciprocal of total asset turnover, so higher values mean lower asset efficiency. Capital-intensive industries naturally show larger ratios.

name: Return on Net Assets (RONA)
description: Computes return on net assets as net income divided by the sum of fixed assets and net working capital. It measures how efficiently a company generates profit from the capital tied up in operating assets.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Net working capital already nets current liabilities against current assets, so it should not double-count liabilities.

name: Cash Flow Margin
description: Computes the cash flow margin as operating cash flow divided by revenue. It shows how effectively sales are converted into actual operating cash, complementing accrual-based profit margins.
notes: The result is a decimal fraction (multiply by 100 for percent). Because it uses cash flow rather than net income, it is less affected by non-cash accounting items like depreciation.

name: Net Debt to EBITDA
description: Computes the net-debt-to-EBITDA ratio as total debt minus cash and equivalents, divided by EBITDA. It measures how many years of current earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization would be needed to repay net debt.
notes: Cash is subtracted to reflect debt that could be repaid immediately; a negative result means cash exceeds debt. Lenders often set covenant limits such as 3x or 4x.

name: Fixed-Charge Coverage Ratio
description: Computes the fixed-charge coverage ratio as EBIT plus lease payments, divided by interest expense plus lease payments. It measures a firm's ability to cover fixed financing charges, including both interest and lease obligations.
notes: Lease payments are added back to earnings and included in the charges because they are committed fixed costs; a higher ratio indicates a greater ability to meet obligations. It extends the interest coverage ratio to include leases.

name: Operating Cash Flow (Indirect Method)
description: Converts net income to operating cash flow by adding back non-cash charges and subtracting the growth in working capital.
notes: Other non-cash items (impairments, share-based pay) are added back the same way.

name: Free Cash Flow (Simple)
description: Gives the cash left after the investment needed to keep and grow the business.
notes: The quantity many investors watch most closely.

name: EBITDA (Earnings before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortisation)
description: Adds depreciation and amortisation back to operating profit (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation).
notes: A rough proxy for operating cash flow, but it ignores capital spending and working capital.

name: Cash Coverage Ratio
description: Divides EBITDA by interest expense, showing how many times cash earnings cover interest.
notes: Complements the interest coverage ratio, which uses EBIT.

name: Working Capital Turnover
description: Measures revenue generated per unit of net working capital.
notes: Very high values can signal too little working capital to support growth.

name: Altman Z″-Score (Non-Manufacturers and Emerging Markets)
description: Predicts financial distress for non-manufacturing firms (Altman 1995), without the sales-based term.
notes: Above 2.6 safe, 1.1–2.6 grey zone, below 1.1 distress.

name: Beneish M-Score (Earnings Manipulation)
description: Scores the likelihood that a company has manipulated its earnings from eight year-on-year ratios (Beneish 1999).
notes: Scores above −1.78 suggest a likely manipulator; the model flagged Enron before its collapse.

name: Accruals Ratio (Balance-Sheet Quality)
description: Measures how much of earnings is not backed by cash, relative to assets.
notes: High accruals tend to predict weaker future earnings (Sloan 1996).

name: Effective Tax Rate
description: Divides the income tax expense by pre-tax profit.
notes: Differs from the statutory rate because of credits, foreign income and permanent differences.

name: Goodwill on Acquisition
description: Gives goodwill: the price paid in excess of the fair value of identifiable net assets (IFRS 3 / ASC 805).
notes: A negative result is a bargain purchase, recognised as a gain.

name: Percentage-of-Completion Revenue
description: Recognises revenue on a long-term contract in proportion to the costs incurred (input method, IFRS 15).
notes: Subtract revenue recognised in earlier periods for this period's amount.

name: Effective-Interest Amortisation: Interest Expense

variables.label: Carrying amount at start of period

description: Gives the interest expense for a period under the effective-interest method (IFRS 9): carrying amount times the market rate at issue.
notes: The difference from the coupon paid amortises the discount or premium.

name: Effective-Interest Amortisation: New Carrying Amount

variables.label: Carrying amount at start of period

description: Rolls the carrying amount of a bond forward one period: interest expense added, coupon paid subtracted.
notes: Reaches face value exactly at maturity.

name: Deferred Tax from a Temporary Difference
description: Gives the deferred tax liability (positive) or asset (negative) on the difference between the accounting and tax values of an asset (IAS 12).
notes: Use the tax rate expected when the difference reverses.

name: Impairment Loss

variables.label: Fair value less costs of disposal

description: Gives the write-down when the carrying amount exceeds the recoverable amount, the higher of fair value less costs of disposal and value in use (IAS 36).

name: Lease Liability (Present Value of Payments in Advance)
description: Gives the initial lease liability for payments made at the start of each period, discounted at the lessee's borrowing rate (IFRS 16).
notes: The right-of-use asset starts at this amount plus initial direct costs.

name: Foreign-Currency Translation Gain or Loss
description: Gives the exchange gain (positive) or loss on a foreign-currency receivable when it is remeasured at the closing rate (IAS 21).
notes: For payables the sign is reversed.

name: Days Cash on Hand
description: Gives how many days an organisation could keep paying its operating costs from cash alone.
notes: Hospitals, universities and non-profits track this closely.

name: Book-to-Bill Ratio
description: Divides new orders by billings in the same period; above 1 means demand is growing faster than output.
notes: Watched closely in the semiconductor and capital-goods industries.

name: Capital Expenditure Coverage Ratio
description: Divides operating cash flow by capital spending; above 1 means investment is self-funded.
notes: Growth companies often run below 1 for years.

name: Revenue per Employee
description: Divides revenue by the number of full-time-equivalent staff.
notes: Useful within an industry; software firms reach several times the figures of retailers.

name: Program Expense Ratio (Non-Profit)
description: Gives the share of a charity's spending that goes to its programmes rather than administration and fundraising.
notes: Watchdogs often look for at least 65–75 %.
